chapter.name: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

questions.q: At a Diwali stall in Pune, Riya places a round glass bottle filled with water on a price list and the numbers look larger through it. Which idea from the early history of lenses does this show?
questions.a: A curved, clear object makes small things look bigger
o: A curved, clear object makes small things look bigger
Water makes printed ink spread out and grow wider
Any flat sheet of glass on a page enlarges the letters
The bottle traps air, and the air makes letters swell

questions.q: For a science wall in Kochi, four students each write one sentence about Robert Hooke's cork slice. Which sentence is fully supported by the chapter's account?
questions.a: He gave the name now used for the basic unit of life
o: He gave the name now used for the basic unit of life
He proved that every living being is made of cells
He made the first tool ever to make things look bigger
He saw a nucleus inside every compartment of the cork

questions.q: At its strongest, Robert Hooke's microscope made things look 300 times bigger. A cork compartment 0.08 mm across would then look ___ mm wide. (Write the number in digits.)

(a) Kabir has two pieces of glass. Piece M is thick in the middle and thin at the edge; piece R is equally thick everywhere. Which piece has the shape that gave the lens its name, and what was the name based on?
(b) Kabir's friend says, 'A lens is called a lens because it makes things look bigger.' Using (a), correct her.
questions.a: (a) Piece M. Its shape is like a lentil seed (thick in the middle, thin at the edge), and the lens was named after this lentil shape. (b) The name comes from the shape, not from what the glass does. Making small things look bigger is the job a curved piece of glass does; 'lens' only records that the glass looked like a lentil seed.
s: (a) piece M; the name comes from its lentil-seed shape
(b) correction: the name records the shape, while enlarging is what the curved glass does

questions.q:
(a) Robert Hooke drew what he saw through his microscope. Leela looks at an onion peel and draws round cells with wide gaps between them, because she 'knows cells are round'. Which part of Hooke's way of working did she not follow?
(b) Using (a), say what her drawing should have shown, according to the chapter's observation of onion peel.
questions.a: (a) She drew what she expected, not what she actually saw; Hooke drew carefully what he observed. (b) Nearly rectangular cells, closely arranged without any space between them.
s: (a) she drew from expectation instead of from careful observation
(b) nearly rectangular cells packed with no gaps

questions.q: Meher claims: 'Without the improvement of lenses over time, neither Hooke's cork drawings nor Leeuwenhoek's description of bacteria would have been possible.' Is her claim right, wrong or partly right? Use the chapter's account to decide.
questions.a: Right. The chapter says lenses were improved over time to become more powerful, and this led from simple magnifying glasses to microscopes. Hooke's cork drawings were made with a microscope that magnified 200 to 300 times, and Leeuwenhoek could clearly see bacteria and blood cells only because he made better lenses and built more useful microscopes. So both depended on improved lenses.
s: Verdict: right
Hooke's cork view needed a microscope, which came from improved lenses
Leeuwenhoek's bacteria came from his better lenses

questions.q:
Each observation in Column I was made with one of the tools in Column II. Match them.
Column I | Column II
1. Letters on a book page look bigger through a round container | a. Hooke's microscope
2. An ant's legs are seen in more detail at a picnic | b. Leeuwenhoek's microscope
3. A thin cork slice shows honeycomb-like compartments | c. a water-filled round-bottom flask
4. Bacteria and blood cells are clearly described for the first time | d. a hand magnifying glass

Through Robert Hooke's microscope, which made things look 200 to 300 times bigger, a cork compartment appears 15 mm wide.
(a) What is its smallest possible actual width?
(b) What is its largest possible actual width?
(c) Why can you give only a range and not one exact value?
questions.a: (a) 15 / 300 = 0.05 mm. (b) 15 / 200 = 0.075 mm. (c) The microscope's enlargement is given only as 200 to 300 times, so the actual width could be anywhere from 0.05 mm (if it was 300 times) to 0.075 mm (if it was 200 times).
s: (c) the enlargement is a range, 200 to 300 times

questions.q:
A Class 8 quiz card makes three statements about Robert Hooke's cork observation.
Statement 1: He saw the thin cork slice as many small, empty spaces that reminded him of a honeycomb.
Statement 2: His skill as an artist did not matter, because Micrographia printed photographs of what he saw.
Statement 3: His naming of each space a 'cell' was the first time the word was used in science for the basic unit of life.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: True or False? 'Hooke called the compartments in cork cells because, like the cells of an onion peel, each one was full of living material.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Hooke saw that the cork was made of many small, empty spaces that reminded him of a honeycomb, and he called each small space a cell. He did not see living material inside them; the word cell named the empty compartments he drew.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Hooke saw empty, honeycomb-like spaces and named each space a cell

questions.q:
A science club in Bhopal views a thin cork slice through one microscope at three settings. Each compartment is about 0.05 mm across. The table gives how wide a strip of the slice fits in the view at each setting.
Setting | Times bigger | Width of the slice seen in the view
Low | 100 | 1.2 mm
Medium | 200 | 0.6 mm
High | 400 | 0.3 mm
For poster 1, the club needs each compartment to look at least 8 mm wide AND at least 10 compartments side by side in the view, to show the honeycomb pattern.
(a) How wide does one compartment look at each setting?
(b) How many compartments fit across the view at each setting?
(c) Which setting meets both needs of poster 1? Use (a) and (b).
(d) Poster 2 must show the wall of a single compartment, looking at least 15 mm wide. Which setting should the club use now, and what does the pair of posters show about choosing the 'strongest' setting?
questions.a: (a) Low: 0.05 x 100 = 5 mm; medium: 0.05 x 200 = 10 mm; high: 0.05 x 400 = 20 mm. (b) Low: 1.2 / 0.05 = 24; medium: 0.6 / 0.05 = 12; high: 0.3 / 0.05 = 6. (c) Medium only: 10 mm (at least 8) and 12 compartments (at least 10). Low fails on size (5 mm) and high fails on the pattern (only 6 compartments). (d) High: 20 mm, the only setting at least 15 mm. The best setting depends on the purpose: more enlargement shows one compartment better but fewer of them, so the strongest setting is not always the right one.
s: (a) 5 mm, 10 mm and 20 mm
(b) 24, 12 and 6 compartments
(c) medium only, as low is too small and high shows too few
(d) high for poster 2; the right setting depends on the purpose

questions.q: At 100 times, a pond organism looks 6 mm long through Leela's school microscope. She turns it to 400 times. How long will the organism now look?
questions.a: 24 mm
o: 24 mm
306 mm
1.5 mm

questions.q:
Robert Hooke was a careful observer and a skilled artist, and his 1665 book Micrographia showed detailed drawings of tiny things seen through his microscope.
(a) What could a reader in 1665, who owned no microscope, do with Micrographia that a written description alone would not let her do?
(b) Why did the drawings need both of Hooke's skills, and not only one of them?
questions.a: (a) She could see for herself what the tiny things looked like, for example the honeycomb-like compartments of cork, things people had never seen before, instead of only imagining them from words. (b) Careful observation made sure he noticed the real details correctly; artistic skill let him put those details on paper accurately. A careless observer would draw wrong details well, and a poor artist would spoil correct observations, so the drawings were trustworthy only with both.
s: (a) readers could see what the tiny things looked like, not just read about them
(b) observation gets the details right; drawing skill records them accurately

questions.q: A grandmother in Mysuru reads a tiny medicine label with a magnifying glass. A scientist in a laboratory looks at blood cells with a microscope. Give one way the two tools are alike and one way they differ in what they let the user see.
questions.a: Alike: both use lenses to make small things look bigger. Different: the magnifying glass only shows more detail of things we can already see (the label's letters), while the microscope, with its more powerful, improved lenses, shows things too small to be seen with the naked eye at all, such as blood cells.
s: Alike: both use lenses to make things look bigger
Differ: the microscope is more powerful and shows things invisible to the naked eye

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'Because he made better lenses, which let him build more useful microscopes.' Write a question about early microscopes for which this is the correct answer, and explain how this answer links to what that scientist is remembered for.
questions.a: Example question: 'Why could Antonie van Leeuwenhoek clearly see bacteria and blood cells?' (or 'How did Leeuwenhoek become the first to clearly describe tiny living things?'). Link: his better lenses and microscopes let him be the first to clearly see and describe tiny living things like bacteria and blood cells, which is why he is known as the Father of Microbiology.
s: A question about Leeuwenhoek seeing bacteria or blood cells
Better lenses led to more useful microscopes
This let him first describe bacteria, so he is the Father of Microbiology

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Robert Hooke is known as the Father of Microbiology.
Reason (R): Hooke's book Micrographia showed detailed drawings of tiny things that people had never seen before.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Plan a five-station demonstration for Class 6 visitors that leads them from 'things can look bigger' to 'there is a hidden living world'. You may use only things named in this chapter: a round-bottom flask filled with water, a hand magnifying glass, a foldable paper microscope, a school microscope (100 to 400 times), and the story of Hooke and Leeuwenhoek. For each station give what is shown, what the visitor observes, and the idea it adds to the one before.
questions.a: A sound plan, in an order that builds up: (1) Water-filled round flask on an open book: the letters look larger; a curved, clear object acts like a magnifying glass. (2) Hand magnifying glass on an ant: its body parts are seen in more detail; a lens shows more of things we can already see. (3) Foldable paper microscope on an onion peel: nearly rectangular cells packed with no gaps; a microscope shows things too small for the naked eye, and a low-cost one makes this possible for many people, though with less detail. (4) School microscope, 100 to 400 times, on a drop of pond water: Amoeba, Paramecium or algae; tiny living things are present that the eye cannot see at all. (5) History panel: Hooke's microscope (200 to 300 times) showed empty compartments in cork that he named cells in 1665, and Leeuwenhoek's better lenses let him first clearly describe bacteria and blood cells, so he is called the Father of Microbiology; improving lenses is what opened the hidden world.
s: Station 1: water-filled flask, letters enlarged, curved object magnifies
Station 2: hand lens on an ant, more detail of a visible thing
Station 3: paper microscope on onion peel, cells too small for the eye
Station 4: school microscope on pond water, hidden living things
Station 5: Hooke and Leeuwenhoek, improved lenses opened the hidden world

questions.q: Arjun's hand magnifying glass makes things look about 5 times bigger. He can make out a thing only if it looks at least 1 mm across. Through the glass he looks at an ant's leg 0.3 mm thick and at a cheek cell 0.05 mm across. What will he see?
questions.a: The ant's leg, but not the cheek cell
o: The ant's leg, but not the cheek cell
Both, since any lens makes things look bigger
Neither, since 5 times is too little for anything
The cheek cell, but not the ant's leg

questions.q: A school poster says: 'In 1665 Robert Hooke invented the lens. Using it, he became the first to see bacteria, which he called cells.' The poster has three errors. Find each one and correct it.
questions.a: Error 1: Hooke did not invent the lens. People long ago found that a curved, lentil-shaped piece of glass made things look bigger, and lenses were improved over time; in 1665 Hooke published Micrographia with drawings made through his microscope. Error 2: Hooke was not the first to see bacteria; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to clearly see and describe bacteria and blood cells. Error 3: Hooke's 'cells' were not bacteria; he used the word for the many small, empty, honeycomb-like spaces he saw in a thin slice of cork.
s: Error 1 corrected: the lens was known long before; Hooke used a microscope
Error 2 corrected: Leeuwenhoek first clearly described bacteria
Error 3 corrected: 'cell' named the empty spaces in cork, not bacteria

questions.q:
A government school in Wardha has Rs 6,000 for its 'invisible world' corner and 30 students in Class 8. Plan P: one laboratory microscope that magnifies 100 to 400 times, costing Rs 6,000. Plan Q: foldable paper microscopes at Rs 200 each, one per student, each making things look about 140 times bigger. A student can make out a detail only if it looks at least 1 mm across. A practical period lasts 40 minutes.
(a) What does Plan Q cost in total, and how wide does an onion peel cell 0.1 mm across look through one paper microscope?
(b) A bacterium is about 0.003 mm long. Can each plan show it? Show your working.
(c) Under Plan P, if every student gets an equal turn in one period, about how long is each turn?
(d) The teacher's main aim this term is that every student prepares and studies her own onion peel and cheek cell slides, but she also wants the class to see bacteria. Recommend a plan, and say what the class gives up with your choice.
questions.a: (a) 30 x Rs 200 = Rs 6,000; the cell looks 0.1 x 140 = 14 mm wide. (b) Plan Q: 0.003 x 140 = 0.42 mm, less than 1 mm, so no. Plan P: 0.003 x 400 = 1.2 mm, at least 1 mm, so yes. (c) 40 / 30 = about 1.3 minutes each. (d) Plan Q fits the main aim: every student can work on her own slide for the whole period, and the cells look 14 mm wide, enough to see; the chapter notes paper microscopes give less detail but make the microscopic world accessible to many. What is given up: bacteria (0.42 mm) cannot be seen, so the class would need to see them another way. (Plan P accepted only if the answer weighs that it shows bacteria at 1.2 mm but gives each student only about 1.3 minutes and no slide of her own.)
s: (b) Plan Q 0.42 mm, no; Plan P 1.2 mm, yes
(c) about 1.3 minutes per student
(d) a plan chosen for the stated aim, naming what is given up

questions.q: A student writes in a quiz: 'The microscope was invented by one person, Robert Hooke, in 1665, and nothing important about it has changed since then.' Use five points from the chapter, including at least two of the numbers it gives, to show why this is wrong.
questions.a: Any five: (1) Long before 1665, people found that a curved, lentil-shaped piece of glass made small things look bigger, and lenses were then improved over time to become more powerful. (2) The tools developed step by step, from simple magnifying glasses to microscopes, not in one go. (3) Hooke used 'a tool we now call a microscope' that made things look 200 to 300 times bigger; the chapter does not say he invented it. (4) Around the same time, in the 1660s, Leeuwenhoek made better lenses and built more useful microscopes, and was the first to clearly see bacteria and blood cells. (5) Microscopes kept changing: a school microscope magnifies 100 to 400 times, low-cost foldable paper microscopes now make the microscopic world accessible to many people, and an electron microscope magnifies a cell about 10,00,000 times to show structures inside it.
s: Lenses were known earlier and improved over time
Magnifying glasses came before microscopes: a gradual change
Hooke used a 200 to 300 times microscope; no claim he invented it
Leeuwenhoek improved lenses and microscopes in the 1660s
Later change: 100 to 400 times, paper microscope, about 10,00,000 times

questions.q:
(a) Differentiate between the cell membrane and the cell wall by saying what each one does.
(b) Using (a), name one cell from this chapter's activities that has only the first of these two layers, and one that has both.
questions.a: (a) The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus, separates one cell from another and, being porous, lets in materials needed for life and lets out waste. The cell wall is an extra outer layer in plant cells that gives rigidity and strength. (b) A human cheek cell has only a cell membrane; an onion peel cell has both a cell membrane and a cell wall.
s: (a) membrane controls entry and exit and separates cells; wall gives rigidity and strength
(b) cheek cell: membrane only; onion peel cell: both

questions.q: Ayaan prepares a cheek cell slide but forgets to add methylene blue. Everything else is done correctly. What is he most likely to notice?
questions.a: The cells are hard to make out, as there is little contrast
o: The cells are hard to make out, as there is little contrast
The cells dry out within seconds, as nothing stops drying
The cells look nearly rectangular instead of polygon-shaped
Each cell has lost its nucleus, as the stain forms the nucleus

questions.q:
Read three statements about the parts of a cell.
Statement 1: The cell wall, not the cell membrane, controls which materials enter and leave a cell.
Statement 2: Cytoplasm contains compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts.
Statement 3: In animal cells, vacuoles are usually absent, and if present they are usually small.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Under the microscope, Tara counts onion peel cells. Along the length of a straight strip, 10 cells end to end cover 2.4 mm; across the strip, 4 cells side by side cover 0.4 mm.
(i) Find the length and the width of one cell.
(ii) How many times longer than wide is a cell, and does this fit the chapter's description of onion peel cells?
(iii) Why can Tara simply divide the strip's length by the number of cells, using what the chapter says about how these cells are arranged?
questions.a: (i) Length = 2.4 / 10 = 0.24 mm; width = 0.4 / 4 = 0.1 mm. (ii) 0.24 / 0.1 = 2.4 times longer than wide, which fits the 'nearly rectangular' cells the chapter describes. (iii) Onion peel cells are closely arranged without any space between them, so the whole length is made of cells alone; if there were gaps, dividing would give too large a value.
s: (i) 0.24 mm long and 0.1 mm wide
(ii) 2.4 times; fits nearly rectangular cells
(iii) cells packed with no gaps, so the length is all cells

questions.q: In a thought experiment, a single cell is gently split into two halves of equal size. Only the half that holds the nucleus goes on growing; the other half soon stops all activity. Which job of the nucleus does this best show?
questions.a: It regulates the cell's activities and growth
o: It regulates the cell's activities and growth
It lets needed materials in and sends waste out
It gives the cell its rigidity and its strength
It stores substances and maintains cell shape

questions.q: Sana writes in her notes: 'Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a cell membrane.' Is her claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain, and rewrite the sentence correctly.
questions.a: Partly right (or wrong, since the key word 'instead' is false). It is correct that plant cells, such as onion peel cells, have a cell wall. But the wall is an extra outer layer, not a replacement: plant cells still have a cell membrane inside the wall, which encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus and controls the entry and exit of materials. Correct sentence: 'Plant cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane.'
s: Verdict: partly right or wrong, either with the correction that the membrane is still present
The wall is an extra layer; the membrane is still present and does its job
Corrected sentence: wall outside the membrane

questions.q:
A class compares a cell to a school. Match each cell part in Column I to the school role in Column II that does the same kind of job.
Column I | Column II
1. Nucleus | a. The gate that lets supplies in and sends rubbish out
2. Cell membrane | b. The principal's office that directs all activities and growth
3. Cytoplasm | c. A storeroom that holds supplies and waste and keeps the building's shape
4. Vacuole | d. The halls and rooms where most of the day's work happens

(a) Most of a cell's life processes take place in its cytoplasm. Why, then, does the cytoplasm need to hold compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts?
(b) Using (a), explain why the cell membrane has to be porous rather than completely sealed.
questions.a: (a) These compounds are the materials that the life processes in the cytoplasm use and work on. (b) As the processes go on, fresh materials have to keep coming in and the waste they make has to leave; a porous membrane allows the entry of materials essential for life processes and the exit of waste, which a sealed bag could not do.
s: (a) the compounds are the materials the life processes in the cytoplasm use
(b) materials must keep entering and waste leaving, so the membrane must be porous

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under a microscope, the cells of an onion peel look firm and are packed closely together.
Reason (R): The cell wall in plant cells provides rigidity and strength.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A biology club looks at four cell samples, W, X, Y and Z, and records what it sees.
Sample | Cell wall | Rod-shaped bodies | Vacuole
W | present | present, green | one large, empty-looking space
X | absent | absent | none seen
Y | present | present, not green | one large, empty-looking space
Z | absent | absent | one small vacuole
All four show a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
(a) Which samples come from a plant? Give the feature that tells you.
(b) What are the rod-shaped bodies in Y, and what are they most likely doing there?
(c) Which sample could carry out photosynthesis? Explain.
(d) The club has time to show a younger class only one slide, on which it will point out all three extra plant-cell structures. Both plant samples have all three, but colourless rod-shaped bodies are very hard for beginners to spot. Which sample should they choose, and what would the class miss if the other plant sample were used?
questions.a: (a) W and Y, because they have a cell wall (an extra outer layer of plant cells), and also plastids and a large vacuole. (b) They are plastids that are not green, as in non-green plant parts, where plastids help store substances. (c) W, because its green rod-shaped bodies are chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll and help in photosynthesis. (d) Sample W. Its plastids are green, so beginners can find them easily, and they are chloroplasts, so the class can also be told how the cell makes food. With Y, the colourless plastids would be hard to spot and the class would miss the link between plastids and photosynthesis. X and Z are not plant cells.
s: (a) W and Y, because of the cell wall
(b) non-green plastids that store substances
(c) W, its chloroplasts contain chlorophyll
(d) choose W: its plastids are easy to see and show food-making; Y's are hard to spot

questions.q: True or False? 'Glycerin is put on the onion peel so that the cells take on a colour and can be seen clearly.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The colour comes from the stain, safranin, which gives the cells a pinkish colour. Glycerin is added to prevent the cells from drying and to improve clarity for better viewing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: safranin colours the cells; glycerin prevents drying and improves clarity

questions.q: Suppose the cell membrane of a cheek cell stopped being porous and let nothing pass through it. Going by the jobs of the cell parts, what would go wrong first?
questions.a: Needed materials could not enter, and waste would stay inside
o: Needed materials could not enter, and waste would stay inside
The cell would lose its rigidity, and the cheek lining would droop
The cell's food-making in its green bodies would come to a stop
The cell would lose control over its growth and other activities

questions.q:
Three students explain why onion peel cells look firm and packed closely together.
P: 'Because onion cells have no nucleus to make them soft.'
Q: 'Because the cell wall gives the cells rigidity and strength.'
R: 'Because the cell membrane is porous.'
Which explanation is best? Say what is wrong with each of the other two.
questions.a: Q is best: the chapter says the cell wall provides rigidity and strength, which is why plant cells are arranged compactly and look firm. P is wrong because onion peel cells do have a nucleus. R states a true fact (the membrane is porous, letting materials in and waste out), but porosity does not explain firmness or close packing.
s: Q is best: the cell wall gives rigidity and strength
P is wrong: onion cells have a nucleus
R is true but does not explain firmness

questions.q: Amit's leaf cell loses most of the contents of its large vacuole, and under the microscope the cell looks shrunken and out of form. Of the vacuole's jobs, the one that has failed most visibly is maintaining the cell's ___.
questions.a: shape

questions.q:
(a) Sunil forgets the glycerin when making his cheek cell slide and looks at it 20 minutes later. What has most likely happened to the cells, and why?
(b) His friend added glycerin but did not wipe the extra glycerin from around the coverslip with blotting paper. Comparing the two slips, which one harms the cells themselves, and which only affects how tidy the slide is? Explain using (a).
questions.a: (a) The cells have dried out, because glycerin is added to prevent the cells from drying. (b) Sunil's slip harms the cells, since without glycerin they dry. His friend's slip leaves extra glycerin around the edges, which only makes the slide messy; the glycerin is still over the cells, so they are kept from drying.
s: (a) the cells dried, as glycerin prevents drying
(b) missing glycerin harms the cells; unwiped extra glycerin only makes the slide untidy

questions.q: A labelled drawing of a cheek cell shows: part 1, the thin outer layer; part 2, the round structure in the middle; part 3, the region between part 1 and part 2. A student writes, 'Most of the cell's life processes take place in part 2.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: Part 3 is where most life processes take place; part 2 regulates them
o: Part 3 is where most life processes take place; part 2 regulates them
Part 1 is where most life processes take place, as it lets materials in
The sentence is right, as part 2 carries out every process of the cell
Part 2 only stores waste, so the processes happen in parts 1 and 3

questions.q:
A potato is a non-green, underground part of a plant used to store food.
(a) What job would the plastids in its cells most likely be doing?
(b) Why would these cells not be able to make food by photosynthesis, even though they have plastids?
questions.a: (a) In non-green parts, plastids help in the storage of substances, so in a potato they would mostly be storing substances. (b) Photosynthesis needs chloroplasts, the plastids that contain green chlorophyll. The potato's plastids are not green, so they lack chlorophyll and cannot make food by photosynthesis.
s: (a) storage of substances
(b) no chloroplasts with chlorophyll, which photosynthesis needs

questions.q:
Priya's practical record for the onion peel activity reads:
Step 1: Pulled the thin, transparent layer from the inner surface of an onion piece with forceps.
Step 2: Placed the peel in a few drops of safranin for 30 seconds.
Step 3: Moved the peel straight from the safranin onto the glass slide.
Step 4: Added a drop of glycerin and dropped the coverslip flat on top in one go.
Observation: dark red patches cover almost the whole slide, two round bright circles sit near one corner, and the cells are hard to see.
(a) Which steps did she carry out correctly?
(b) Explain the dark red patches and say what she should have done.
(c) Explain the round bright circles and say how to avoid them.
(d) Priya has time to redo only one of her two slips before the class ends. Which should she fix, and why does the other matter less for this slide?
questions.a: (a) Steps 1 and 2. (b) Extra stain was left on the peel because she did not rinse it; she should have transferred the peel with a thin brush to a petri dish of water to remove the extra stain before mounting. (c) They are trapped air bubbles, from dropping the coverslip flat at once; the coverslip should be lowered slowly with the help of a needle. (d) The rinsing: the extra stain darkens almost the whole slide, so no part shows the cells clearly. The two bubbles sit in one corner, so she could still look at the cells in the rest of the slide.
s: (a) Steps 1 and 2 correct
(b) unrinsed extra stain; rinse in water first
(c) air bubbles; lower the coverslip slowly with a needle
(d) fix the rinsing: the stain spoils almost the whole slide, the bubbles only one corner

questions.q: For a science fair in Indore, Riya builds a model of a leaf cell from: (1) a stiff cardboard box; (2) a plastic sheet with tiny holes, lining the inside of the box; (3) clear jelly filling the box; (4) a plain rubber ball in the middle; (5) round green beads scattered in the jelly; (6) a large water-filled balloon taking up much of the space. Judge her model: for five of the materials, say which cell part it stands for, whether the material suits that part's job, and what you would change if it does not.
questions.a: Any five, each with part, judgement and fix where needed: (1) The stiff box is the cell wall: a good choice, as the wall gives rigidity and strength. (2) The plastic sheet with holes is the cell membrane: good, as the membrane encloses the cell and is porous, letting needed materials in and waste out; it correctly sits inside the wall. (3) The jelly is the cytoplasm: it fills the space between membrane and nucleus, but the model should show that it holds compounds (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, mineral salts) and other components, since most life processes take place there; add small pieces in the jelly. (4) The ball is the nucleus: its place is right, but it should be wrapped in a thin layer, as the nucleus is covered by a thin membrane. (5) The green beads are chloroplasts: their colour suits chlorophyll, but plastids are rod-shaped, so rod-shaped green pieces would be better. (6) The balloon is the vacuole: a good choice, as a large, empty-looking space that stores substances and keeps the cell's shape.
s: First material: part, judgement against its job
Second material: part, judgement against its job
Third material: part, judgement against its job
A fix for a poor choice, such as rod-shaped plastids or a membrane round the nucleus
Fifth point: part and judgement, with the vacuole or wall linked to shape and strength

questions.q:
Two unlabelled drawings are given.
Drawing X: a polygon-shaped cell bounded by a thin outer layer, with cytoplasm, a round nucleus in the middle and one small vacuole.
Drawing Y: a nearly rectangular cell with a thick outer layer around a thin layer, cytoplasm, a nucleus, several green rod-shaped bodies and one large empty-looking space filling much of the cell.
(a) Decide which drawing is a plant cell and which an animal cell.
(b)-(d) Give three pieces of evidence for your decision, naming each structure and its function.
(e) Explain why the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus seen in both drawings, and the shape of each cell, cannot be used as evidence.
questions.a: (a) X is an animal cell; Y is a plant cell. (b) Y has a thick outer layer, the cell wall, outside the cell membrane; the wall gives rigidity and strength, and X has none. (c) Y has green rod-shaped bodies, chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll and help in photosynthesis; X has none. (d) Y has a large vacuole that stores substances, removes waste and maintains the cell's shape; X's vacuole is small, as in animal cells, where vacuoles are absent or small. (e) The membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus are the basic parts of every cell, so they are found in both kinds and do not tell them apart. Shape is not reliable either: plant cells may be rectangular, elongated, oval or even tube-like, so a cell's outline alone does not decide plant or animal.
s: (a) X animal, Y plant
(b) cell wall in Y with its function
(c) chloroplasts in Y with their function
(d) large vacuole in Y versus small in X, with its function
(e) the three basic parts are shared, and plant cells vary in shape, so neither tells them apart

questions.q: A fish egg cell divides into 2 cells; then every cell divides into 2 again, and so on. If every cell divides in each round, how many cells will there be after 5 rounds?

(a) Inner cheek cells are thin and flat. What job in the mouth does this shape suit?
(b) Using (a), explain why a lining made of loosely arranged spindle-shaped cells would do this job poorly.
questions.a: (a) They form a protective lining on the inner surface of the cheek. (b) A lining has to cover the surface; thin, flat cells can spread over it, while spindle-shaped cells are built to contract and relax (as in the food pipe), and loosely arranged ones would leave the surface poorly covered.
s: (a) a protective lining on the inner surface of the cheek
(b) flat cells cover a surface; spindle cells suit contracting, and loose ones leave it poorly covered

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A grown-up human is a multicellular organism.
Reason (R): The life of a human begins with a single cell, the egg, which divides again and again to form a very large number of cells.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A teacher hands out four cards, each describing a group of cells but not saying where it is found.
Card | Description
K | thin, flat cells joined edge to edge in a sheet
L | very long cells with many branches
M | thin, flexible, spindle-shaped cells in a group that tightens and loosens in waves
N | plant cells joined into long tubes running through the plant
(a) Which card describes nerve cells, and how does their shape help them do their job?
(b) Card M's cells are in the tube that leads from the mouth to the stomach. Name the tube and say what M's cells do there.
(c) What does N most likely carry, and why does its shape suit this?
(d) A Class 6 display has room for only two of the four cards, and it must prove that 'the shape of a cell suits its job' holds in plants as well as in animals. Which two cards could it use? Decide, and say why K and M together would not prove the point.
questions.a: (a) Card L. Nerve cells carry messages; their long, branched shape helps them reach different parts of the body and pass on messages quickly. (b) The food pipe. The muscle cells contract and relax in a wave-like manner and push the food down to the stomach. (c) Water: some plant cells form long tubes that help carry water throughout the plant, and a long tube can run from one part of the plant to another. (d) Card N together with any one of K, L or M. N is the only plant card, so it must be one of the two; the other shows an animal (human) cell whose shape suits its job. K and M are both animal cells, so together they say nothing about plants.
s: (a) L, long and branched to reach body parts and pass messages fast
(b) food pipe; contract and relax in waves to push food
(c) water, carried along long tube-like cells
(d) N plus one animal card; K and M are both animal cells

questions.q:
Read three statements about how living bodies are built.
Statement 1: The muscle cells of the food pipe and the cells lining the inner cheek have different shapes because they do different jobs.
Statement 2: A group of similar cells forms a tissue, and different tissues are organised to form an organ.
Statement 3: Every organism is made of many cells, because the life of every organism begins with an egg.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
(a) Riya finds an oval cell in a sample and says it cannot be a plant cell, because onion peel cells are nearly rectangular. What is wrong with her reasoning, according to the chapter?
(b) Using (a), name one structure she could look for that would be better evidence that the cell is from a plant.
questions.a: (a) Plant cells are not all one shape: the chapter says they may be rectangular, elongated, oval or even tube-like, so an oval cell can still be a plant cell. (b) A cell wall (or chloroplasts, or a large vacuole), which plant cells have and animal cells do not.
s: (a) plant cells may be rectangular, elongated, oval or tube-like
(b) a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large vacuole

questions.q: Aman claims: 'All the cells in the human body have the same shape, because they all came from one egg.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Support your verdict with two examples.
questions.a: Wrong. Although a human does begin as one cell, the egg, the cells of the body have different shapes and structures that suit their jobs. For example, a muscle cell is spindle-shaped, while a nerve cell is very long and branched; inner cheek cells are thin and flat. Coming from one egg does not make the cells alike.
s: Verdict: wrong
Example 1 of a different cell shape (muscle cell spindle-shaped)
Example 2 (nerve cell long and branched, or cheek cell thin and flat)

questions.q: While revising, Riya writes: 'The stomach is a tissue, because it is made of cells.' Which correction is best?
questions.a: It is an organ: different tissues are organised to form it
o: It is an organ: different tissues are organised to form it
It is an organ system, since it does a major job on its own
It is a tissue, since any group of cells counts as a tissue
It is a single cell, since it carries out digestion by itself

questions.q: The chapter compares a cell to a brick in a wall. A student stretches this into a 'school building' model: a brick = a cell; a wall of identical bricks = a tissue; a classroom built from brick walls, a wooden door and glass windows = an organ; a whole floor of classrooms working together for teaching = an organ system; the whole school = an organism. Evaluate the model: give three ways in which it matches the levels of organisation and two ways in which it fails to match a living body.
questions.a: Matches (any three): a wall of similar bricks is like a tissue, a group of similar cells; a classroom made of different materials is like an organ, formed when different tissues are organised; a floor of classrooms working together for one major job is like an organ system, several organs performing a major function; the whole school is like the organism, made of all the organ systems together; the brick, like the cell, is the basic unit. Fails (any two): bricks are identical, but cells vary in shape, size and structure to suit their jobs (spindle-shaped muscle cells, long branched nerve cells); a brick is a simple solid block, but a cell is a complex structure whose parts each have a function; a building is put together from outside, but a living body grows from one egg cell that divides repeatedly.
s: Match 1: wall of similar bricks and tissue
Match 2: classroom of different materials and organ
Match 3: floor and organ system, or school and organism
Fail 1: identical bricks versus cells shaped for their jobs
Fail 2: a lifeless block versus a working, dividing cell

questions.q:
Match each problem in Column I with the group of cells in Column II most likely to be at fault.
Column I | Column II
1. Swallowed food stays stuck in the food pipe | a. thin, flat cells that form a lining
2. Messages from the brain reach the toes too slowly | b. very long cells with many branches
3. The inner surface of the cheek is left unprotected | c. spindle-shaped cells that contract and relax in waves
4. A plant's upper leaves get too little water though the soil is wet | d. long, tube-like plant cells
True or False? 'The yolk of an ostrich egg, which can easily be seen without any lens, is just one cell.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the yolk of an ostrich egg is a single cell, the largest known cell in the living world, about 130 mm to 170 mm across. Not every cell is too small to see; this one is far larger than the microscopic cells of the chapter.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the yolk is a single cell, the largest known, about 130 to 170 mm across

questions.q: Show that a whole ostrich egg, with its shell and white, cannot be counted as one single cell, even though its yolk is one.
questions.a: The yolk alone is the single cell, the largest known cell, about 130 mm to 170 mm across. The shell and the white liquid are extra non-cellular material: the shell protects, and the white nourishes the cell during its continued development. So the whole egg is one cell plus material that is not cellular, and it cannot be counted as one cell.
s: Only the yolk is the single cell
The shell and white are non-cellular material that protect and nourish
So the whole egg is a cell plus non-cellular parts, not one cell

questions.q: In a patient, the cells of the stomach's inner lining stop making digestive juices and acid, but the muscle cells of the stomach wall work normally. What is most likely to happen?
questions.a: Food is still churned, but it is broken down less
o: Food is still churned, but it is broken down less
Food is not churned, but juices still break it down
Food can no longer be pushed down the food pipe
Nothing changes, as muscle cells make the juices

questions.q:
(a) Suppose a frog's egg cell simply grew larger and larger without ever dividing. Would the result be a multicellular organism? Explain.
(b) Using (a), state what the egg must do to become a frog made of many cells.
questions.a: (a) No. However large it grew, it would still be one cell; size alone does not make many cells (the ostrich yolk is one cell even at 130 to 170 mm). (b) It must divide repeatedly, so that one cell becomes many and forms a complete multicellular living being.
s: (a) no: growing bigger leaves it one cell
(b) it must divide repeatedly to form many cells

questions.q:
A museum in Chennai is setting up a display called 'From one cell to a whole body'. The draft labels are:
Box 1 | one spindle-shaped muscle cell | label: tissue
Box 2 | a sheet of many similar muscle cells | label: tissue
Box 3 | a stomach | label: organ
Box 4 | food pipe, stomach and intestine together | label: organ
Box 5 | a whole human figure | label: organism
(a) Which two box labels are wrong?
(b) Give the correct label for each and the reason.
(c) A visitor asks why the sheet of muscle cells in Box 2 could not, on its own, do the stomach's job. Answer using the stomach's cells.
(d) The museum can correct only one wrong label before opening day. Which of the two wrong labels would mislead visitors more about how a body is built? Decide, and justify using what each level is made of.
questions.a: (a) Box 1 and Box 4. (b) Box 1 is a cell, the basic unit of life; a tissue is a group of similar cells. Box 4 is an organ system: several organs working together to perform a major function (digestion). (c) The stomach is an organ made of different tissues: its muscle cells churn the food, but other cells in its inner lining produce the digestive juices and acid that break the food down. A sheet of muscle cells alone could churn but not break down food. (d) Either choice earns the mark if justified: Box 1, because calling a single cell a tissue hides the bottom step (a tissue needs a group of similar cells), so every level above is misread; or Box 4, because calling the digestive system an organ hides that several organs must work together for a major function such as digestion.
s: (a) Box 1 and Box 4
(b) Box 1 is a cell; Box 4 is an organ system
(c) muscle cells only churn; lining cells are needed for juices and acid
(d) one label chosen, justified by what that level is made of

questions.q: A poster says 'In plants too, the shape of a cell suits its job.' Which observation supports the poster best?
questions.a: Some plant cells form long tubes that carry water
o: Some plant cells form long tubes that carry water
All plant cells are rectangular, like onion peel cells
Plant cells have a cell wall but animal cells do not
Leaf cells are green as they contain chloroplasts

questions.q:
A muscle cell and a nerve cell both come from the human body.
(i) Describe the shape of each.
(ii) Link each shape to the job the chapter gives it.
(iii) Explain why a nerve cell with a short, spindle shape would do its own job badly.
questions.a: (i) A muscle cell is spindle-shaped (thin and flexible); a nerve cell is very long and has branches. (ii) Muscle cells in the food pipe contract and relax in a wave-like manner to push food down; the nerve cell's long, branched shape helps it reach different parts of the body and pass on messages quickly. (iii) A short spindle could not stretch out to distant body parts or branch to reach many of them, so messages could not be passed on quickly.
s: (i) spindle-shaped versus very long and branched
(ii) muscle cells push food in waves; nerve cells reach far and pass messages fast
(iii) a short spindle could not reach distant parts or pass messages quickly

questions.q:
(a) What do the muscle cells of the food pipe do, and what do the muscle cells of the stomach wall do?
(b) A student says, 'If the food pipe's muscle cells stopped working, the stomach's muscle cells would push the food down instead.' Using (a), explain why this is unlikely.
questions.a: (a) Food pipe: they contract and relax in a wave-like manner, pushing food down to the stomach. Stomach wall: they help churn the food. (b) The stomach-wall muscle cells work on food that is already in the stomach, churning it; they are not in the food pipe, so they cannot push food that is still stuck there.
s: (a) food pipe cells push food in waves; stomach-wall cells churn it
(b) stomach cells act only on food already in the stomach

questions.q: An ostrich egg yolk, a single cell, is 150 mm across. If plant cells 0.05 mm across were laid in a straight row across it, ___ cells would be needed. (Write the number in digits.)

Imagine designing a simple many-celled water creature. It must (i) protect the inner surface of its mouth, (ii) carry messages quickly from its head to its tail, (iii) push food along a tube to its stomach, (iv) break food down inside the stomach, and (v) be built up level by level from cells. For (i) to (iv), choose a kind of cell from this chapter and justify the choice by its shape or job; for (v), show the levels of organisation for its digestive part.
questions.a: (i) Thin, flat cells like inner cheek cells, which form a protective lining. (ii) Long, branched cells like nerve cells, whose shape helps them reach different parts and pass messages quickly. (iii) Thin, flexible, spindle-shaped muscle cells, like those of the food pipe, which contract and relax in waves to push food. (iv) Cells like those in the inner lining of the stomach, which produce digestive juices and acid that break food down, with stomach-wall muscle cells to churn it. (v) Cell (a muscle cell) -> tissue (a group of similar muscle cells) -> organ (a stomach made of different tissues) -> organ system (food tube and stomach working together for digestion) -> organism (the whole creature).
s: (i) flat lining cells for protection
(ii) long, branched nerve-like cells for messages
(iii) spindle-shaped muscle cells to push food
(iv) stomach-lining cells that make juices and acid
(v) cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism in order

questions.q: Kavya rinses the surface of a neem leaf in a few drops of water and looks at a drop under the microscope. She sees rod-shaped cells, each with one long hair-like structure and many small hair-like projections. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.a: Bacteria live on leaves too, not only in soil and water
o: Bacteria live on leaves too, not only in soil and water
They are algae, since anything taken from a leaf is green
They are protozoa, since hair-like parts are used to move
The leaf made them, as microbes cannot travel through air

questions.q:
(a) What do the two parts of the word 'microorganism' mean?
(b) A mushroom is a fungus that you can see and pick up. Using (a), should it be called a microorganism? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 'Micro' means very small and 'organism' means a living being. (b) No. A microorganism is a living thing so small that it cannot be seen with the naked eye. A mushroom is a fungus, but it is easily seen with the naked eye, so it is not a microorganism (only some fungi are microbes).
s: (a) micro = very small; organism = living being
(b) no: a mushroom is visible to the naked eye

questions.q: Neel claims: 'Because microorganisms are found in hot water springs and in snow-cold zones, they must all be one tough kind of living thing that can survive anywhere.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Wrong. The places are real: some microorganisms are found in extreme conditions such as hot water springs and snow-cold zones. But the chapter says that, like plants and animals, microorganisms show great diversity: only some live in extreme places, others at moderate temperatures, and they vary in shape, size and structure (spherical, rod-shaped or irregular) and belong to different groups such as protozoa, algae, fungi and bacteria. So they are not one kind.
s: Verdict: wrong
Only some microbes live in extreme places; others live at moderate temperatures
Microbes show great diversity of shape, size, structure and group

questions.q:
A lemon left in a fruit basket for a week grows a powdery, cotton-like patch.
(a) What has happened to the lemon?
(b) Nobody put anything on the lemon. Where could the cause have come from?
questions.a: (a) It has been infected by microbes (microorganisms), which are growing on it and making it rot. (b) Microorganisms are found everywhere, in water, soil, air and even on some foods, so they could have reached the lemon from the air or from other things it touched.
s: (a) microbes are growing on it
(b) microbes are everywhere, such as in the air

questions.q: Lata is preparing a soil suspension to look for microbes. Which way of working follows the chapter's method?
questions.a: Stir soil in water, let it settle, use a top-layer drop
o: Stir soil in water, let it settle, use a top-layer drop
Pick up moist soil with bare hands so none of it is lost
Put a small lump of dry soil straight onto the glass slide
Stir soil in water and at once take a drop from the bottom

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Nagpur looks at five drops from each sample and records the average number of each kind of organism per drop.
Row | Sample | What they saw | Average per drop
1 | pond water | single cells, irregular shape, moving | 2
2 | pond water | single cells, moving with specialised structures, not green | 3
3 | pond water | single cells, green, moving with specialised structures | 6
4 | soil suspension | branched filaments without chlorophyll, brush-like structure | 1
5 | soil suspension | spherical cells with chlorophyll | 4
6 | soil suspension | rod-shaped cells with one long hair-like structure and many small projections | 12
(a) Name the organisms in rows 1 and 2, and say why row 3 is not a protozoan.
(b) Which row shows a multicellular microorganism, and what tells you it cannot make its own food using sunlight?
(c) In each sample, what fraction of the organisms per drop carry the green pigment needed to make food using sunlight?
(d) The teacher can show only one slide in a 10-minute class, and wants students to see a multicellular microorganism and also living things that can make their own food. A soil suspension must be left to settle for some time before a drop is taken. Which sample should she plan for, and what must she do differently because of it?
questions.a: (a) Row 1: Amoeba; row 2: Paramecium (both protozoa). Row 3 is green because of a green pigment, which fits algae, not a protozoan. (b) Row 4, the mould (a fungus), made of branched filaments; it has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food using sunlight. (c) Pond: 6 of 2 + 3 + 6 = 11, so 6/11 (about 55 per cent). Soil: 4 of 1 + 4 + 12 = 17, so 4/17 (about 24 per cent). (d) The soil suspension: only it shows a multicellular microbe (the mould), and it also has green algae, even though the pond drop has a larger share of food-makers. Because it must settle, she has to prepare it before the class and take the drop from the top layer.
s: (a) Amoeba and Paramecium; row 3 is green, so algae
(b) row 4, mould: branched filaments with no chlorophyll
(c) pond 6/11; soil 4/17
(d) soil, prepared and settled before the class

questions.q: True or False? 'Microorganisms are found only in dirty places such as drains and garbage heaps.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Microorganisms are found almost everywhere: in water, soil and air, on leaves, stems and roots, in food, inside our gut (where bacteria help in digestion), and even in hot water springs and snow-cold zones.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: microbes are found almost everywhere, including clean places and inside our body

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I to the group of microorganisms in Column II it most likely belongs to.
Column I | Column II
1. A single cell moves through a pond drop, its shape irregular and changing | a. bacteria
2. A green film on a pond wall is made of single cells with a green pigment | b. algae
3. Branched filaments without chlorophyll form a cotton-like patch on a forgotten tomato | c. protozoa
4. Spiral cells with one long hair-like structure appear in a soil drop | d. fungi

A student's field note reads only: 'Single cell, moving, irregular shape.' Write (i) a likely place where the sample was collected, (ii) the tool used and roughly how many times it magnifies, and (iii) the organism and its group.
questions.a: (i) Pond water or stagnant water (or a soil suspension, where similar moving organisms are seen). (ii) A microscope, which magnifies 100 to 400 times. (iii) Amoeba, a protozoan.
s: (i) pond or stagnant water
(ii) a microscope, 100 to 400 times
(iii) Amoeba, Protozoa

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A drop of pond water that looks clear to the naked eye has no living things in it.
Reason (R): Microorganisms are so small that they cannot be seen with the naked eye.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
(a) A sample of a plant virus is kept for a week in a clean bottle of water that contains no living cells. Will the number of viruses increase? Explain.
(b) Using (a), explain why a virus cannot spread on a slice of bread by itself the way bread mould does.
questions.a: (a) No. Viruses multiply only when they enter a living cell, and the bottle has none. (b) A virus is acellular: it is not made of cells and cannot grow on its own; it needs to be inside a living host cell to multiply. Bread mould is made of cells (a multicellular fungus), so it can grow over the bread.
s: (a) no: viruses multiply only inside a living cell
(b) a virus is acellular and needs a host cell; mould is made of cells

questions.q:
Read three statements about viruses.
Statement 1: Like bacteria, a virus is made of a single cell.
Statement 2: Viruses multiply only when they enter a living cell.
Statement 3: Viruses infect only humans and animals, never plants.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A school eco-club in Shimla looks at one drop from each of five places under a microscope that magnifies 400 times.
Site | Sample | What was seen in the drop
A | water from the edge of a pond | many cells: some irregular and moving, some green and moving
B | water used to rinse a leaf's surface | a few rod-shaped cells with hair-like projections
C | liquid from inside a jar of salty lime pickle | nothing
D | water from a hot spring, collected on a trip | a few rod-shaped cells
E | one drop of rainwater from a clean steel bowl | nothing
(a) Which sites support the statement 'microorganisms are found almost everywhere', and which result would most surprise someone who thinks microbes need mild conditions?
(b) Explain the result at C using the chapter.
(c) A member says site E proves that rainwater has no microbes. Why is one empty drop not enough to prove this?
(d) To which group do the cells at B most likely belong? Give the clue.
(e) Write one conclusion the whole table supports and one popular idea that site B or D shows to be wrong.
questions.a: (a) A, B and D; the hot spring (D) is the surprise, since the chapter says some microbes live in extreme conditions such as hot water springs. (b) The pickle has a high concentration of salt (with spices) that acts as a preservative and does not allow microorganisms to grow. (c) One drop is a tiny sample; microbes present in small numbers can easily be missed, and the chapter says microbes are found in water and air, so one empty drop cannot rule them out. (d) Bacteria: rod-shaped cells with hair-like projections, as in the soil record. (e) Supported: microorganisms live in many different places, including on leaf surfaces and in a hot spring. Shown wrong: the idea that microbes live only in water and soil (B, a leaf surface) or only in mild conditions (D, a hot spring).
s: (a) A, B and D; the hot spring is the surprise
(b) high salt stops microbes growing in the pickle
(c) one drop is too small a sample to rule microbes out
(d) bacteria: rod-shaped with hair-like projections
(e) a supported conclusion and an idea shown wrong by B or D

questions.q: Riya wants to test whether moisture affects how fast mould grows on bread. Which pair of set-ups is a fair test?
questions.a: Two slices of one loaf, same warm place, one moist and one dry
o: Two slices of one loaf, same warm place, one moist and one dry
A moist slice in a warm place and a dry slice in the refrigerator
A moist slice of bread and a dry chapati side by side on one shelf
One moist slice in a warm place, checked every day for three days

questions.q:
Two students sketch the same single, moving pond cell. Student X labels it Amoeba; student Y labels it Paramecium.
(a) Using the class record of pond water, what feature in the sketch would support X's label?
(b) What feature would support Y's label instead?
questions.a: (a) An irregular shape: the record describes Amoeba as a single moving cell of irregular shape. (b) Specialised structures that it uses to move from one place to another, as the record notes for Paramecium.
s: (a) an irregular shape supports Amoeba
(b) specialised structures used for moving support Paramecium

questions.q:
Five drops from the top layer of a settled soil suspension show 9, 12, 10, 4 and 15 bacteria.
(i) Find the mean number of bacteria per drop.
(ii) Which drop differs most from the mean, and why should a conclusion not rest on any one drop alone?
(iii) A student writes, 'So the beaker contains 10 bacteria.' Correct her.
questions.a: (i) (9 + 12 + 10 + 4 + 15) / 5 = 50 / 5 = 10 per drop. (ii) The drop with 4 (6 below the mean). Counts vary a lot from drop to drop, so one drop could give a misleading picture; the mean of several drops is more reliable. (iii) 10 is the mean for one drop; the beaker holds a great many drops, so it contains far more than 10 bacteria.
s: (i) 50 / 5 = 10 per drop
(ii) the drop with 4; single drops vary, so use several
(iii) 10 is per drop; the beaker holds many drops

questions.q: A health poster says, 'Every microbe is a germ that must be removed from the body.' Which fact from the chapter shows that the poster goes too far?
questions.a: Bacteria in our intestine help in digestion
o: Bacteria in our intestine help in digestion
Microorganisms cannot be seen with the naked eye
Viruses multiply only when they enter a living cell
Pickles stay safe because of their high salt

questions.q:
A family in Jaipur prepares three foods on Sunday and keeps them on the same kitchen shelf.
Food | What went into it
P | lime pickle with a lot of salt and spices
Q | amla murabba with a lot of sugar
R | plain boiled dal with no salt
By Wednesday, R has a cotton-like growth; P and Q look unchanged.
(a) What is the cotton-like growth on R, and how did it get there?
(b) Why did P not spoil?
(c) In Q, what does the job that salt does in P?
(d) Grandmother wants to cut the salt in P to a quarter for health reasons. She can either keep the low-salt pickle on the shelf for months like the usual one, or make a small batch, keep it in the refrigerator and finish it within a few days. Using (b), decide which plan is safer, and say what the other plan risks.
questions.a: (a) It is microbial growth: microorganisms are found everywhere, including the air, and they grew on the dal. (b) The salt and spices act as preservatives; a high concentration of salt does not allow microorganisms to grow. (c) The sugar: a high concentration of sugar also stops microorganisms from growing. (d) The small batch kept cool and eaten within a few days. With a quarter of the salt, the concentration may no longer be high enough to stop microbes, so the pickle loses its protection; keeping it cool (microbes need a suitable temperature to grow well) and short gives them little chance to grow. The shelf plan risks the pickle spoiling with a cotton-like growth, as the dal did.
s: (a) microbes from the air grew on the dal
(b) high salt concentration stops microbes growing
(c) sugar, in high concentration
(d) small cool batch: less salt no longer protects it, so the shelf plan risks spoiling

questions.q: A school microscope magnifies 100 to 400 times. At its highest setting, a bacterium 0.002 mm long would appear ___ mm long. (Write the number in digits.)

Plan a class investigation comparing the microbes in pond water with those in garden soil. Give (a) the steps for preparing the pond water slide, (b) the steps for preparing the soil slide, (c) one safety precaution, (d) what you expect to see in each sample, naming two organisms for each, and (e) why both slides must be seen under a microscope and not a magnifying glass.
questions.a: (a) Collect pond or stagnant water with a teacher or elder; place a drop on a slide with a dropper, put on a coverslip and observe under the microscope. (b) Collect moist soil in a beaker, add water and stir with a glass rod to make a soil suspension, let it settle, take a drop from the top layer, place it on a slide, cover with a coverslip and observe. (c) Do not touch the soil with bare hands: use a spoon or gloves (collect pond water only with an adult's help). (d) Pond water: Amoeba, Paramecium or algae. Soil: bread mould, mould, algae or bacteria. (e) These organisms cannot be seen with the naked eye; a microscope magnifies them 100 to 400 times and makes them visible.
s: (a) pond water slide steps
(b) soil suspension slide steps, drop from the top layer
(c) safety: spoon or gloves, adult help
(d) two expected organisms for each sample
(e) microbes need 100 to 400 times magnification

questions.q: A farmer in Bihar pulls up a cowpea plant and finds small swollen lumps on its roots. She fears the plant is diseased. What is the best advice?
questions.a: Keep it: its lumps hold Rhizobium, which traps air's nitrogen
o: Keep it: its lumps hold Rhizobium, which traps air's nitrogen
Remove it: the lumps are mould feeding on the roots from inside
Keep it: the lumps only store water for the plant on dry days
Remove it: the lumps hold Lactobacillus, which sours the soil

questions.q:
In a dough activity, flour with a pinch of sugar and yeast is kneaded with warm water and kept in a warm place.
(a) Why do the sugar and the warmth help?
(b) Predict what would happen if the same dough were kneaded with ice-cold water and kept in a refrigerator. Explain using (a).
questions.a: (a) Yeast respires and breaks down food (the sugar) to release energy for growth, and yeast grows well in warm conditions. (b) The dough would rise very little, if at all: in the cold, yeast does not grow well, so little carbon dioxide is released to form bubbles and make the dough fluffy.
s: (a) sugar is food for the yeast; yeast grows well when warm
(b) little or no rise, as yeast grows poorly in the cold and makes little carbon dioxide

questions.q:
Read three statements about microbes at work.
Statement 1: In decomposition, microorganisms break complex substances into simpler, nutrient-rich ones.
Statement 2: While fermenting milk, Lactobacillus produces lactic acid, not alcohol.
Statement 3: Rhizobium lives in swollen root nodules of legumes such as peas and lentils.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
(a) What does Lactobacillus produce when it ferments milk, and what gas does yeast release when it breaks down food in dough?
(b) Using (a), explain why curd turns sour while risen dough turns soft and fluffy instead.
questions.a: (a) Lactobacillus produces lactic acid (not alcohol); yeast releases carbon dioxide (with a small amount of alcohol). (b) Lactic acid is what makes curd sour. In dough, the carbon dioxide forms bubbles that make it soft and fluffy, and the little alcohol only gives it a slightly different smell.
s: (a) lactic acid from Lactobacillus; carbon dioxide from yeast
(b) lactic acid makes curd sour; carbon dioxide bubbles make dough fluffy

questions.q: Show that the fruit and vegetable peels buried in soil could not have turned into manure if the soil had contained no microorganisms at all.
questions.a: Manure forms when microorganisms such as fungi and bacteria in the soil act on the plant waste and slowly break it down into simpler, nutrient-rich substances (decomposition). Soil with no microorganisms would have nothing to carry out this breakdown. So the peels would stay as peels and no dark, nutrient-rich manure would form.
s: Manure forms by decomposition by soil fungi and bacteria
Without microbes nothing carries out this breakdown
So the peels would not turn into manure

questions.q: Snehal buries fruit and vegetable peels in a soil-filled container on 1 March. The chapter says the peels turn into manure after 2 to 3 weeks. The earliest date she should check for manure is ___ March. (Write the number in digits.)

Aanandi sets up three test tubes in a warm place, each with a half-inflated balloon on its mouth. Tube A has sugar solution only; tube B has sugar solution and yeast; tube C has yeast in plain water with no sugar. After 3 hours, which result is most likely?
questions.a: B's balloon swells most; A's and C's change little
o: B's balloon swells most; A's and C's change little
B's and C's swell equally, since both contain yeast
A's and B's swell equally, since both contain sugar
All three swell, since warmth expands the air inside

questions.q:
A housing society in Pune collects about 120 kg of kitchen waste a day and must choose one plan.
Plan | What is done | Set-up cost | Saving each month
A | waste mixed with dry leaves and soil in open pits | Rs 5,000 | Rs 3,600 (manure the garden no longer buys)
B | waste fed into a closed tank that keeps air out | Rs 20,000 | Rs 4,500 (cooking gas for the community kitchen)
(a) Plan B's product is a mixture of gases. Name its two main gases.
(b) Find the net saving (total monthly savings minus set-up cost) of each plan after 12 months and after 24 months.
(c) The society expects to use the plan for at least two years. Which plan should it choose, using (b)? Say what it gives up with that choice.
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide and a high proportion of methane (biogas). (b) After 12 months: A = 12 x 3,600 - 5,000 = Rs 38,200; B = 12 x 4,500 - 20,000 = Rs 34,000. After 24 months: A = 24 x 3,600 - 5,000 = Rs 81,400; B = 24 x 4,500 - 20,000 = Rs 88,000. (c) Plan B: it is behind in the first year but ahead by Rs 6,600 after two years, and the gas is a fuel for cooking. It gives up the larger first-year saving and the manure from Plan A, so the garden must keep buying manure to return nutrients to its soil.
s: (a) carbon dioxide and methane
(b) 12 months A Rs 38,200, B Rs 34,000; 24 months A Rs 81,400, B Rs 88,000
(c) Plan B for two years or more, giving up the first-year lead and the manure

questions.q: Dia claims: 'Curd sets because Lactobacillus feeds on the sugar in milk, so cold milk with curd added can never turn even slightly sour.' Is her claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct: Lactobacillus feeds on the sugar in milk (lactose), multiplies and ferments the milk into curd, producing lactic acid. The second part is wrong: in the cold bowl the milk does not curdle, because these bacteria grow well only in warm conditions, but it might still become a little sour, so it is not true that it can never turn slightly sour.
s: Verdict: partly right
Correct part: Lactobacillus feeds on lactose and makes lactic acid
Wrong part: cold milk does not set but may turn a little sour

questions.q:
Match each result in Column I to the microorganism in Column II that brings it about.
Column I | Column II
1. A soft, fluffy loaf of bread | a. bacteria living without oxygen
2. Sour curd from warm milk | b. Rhizobium
3. Nitrogen-rich soil after a lentil crop | c. Lactobacillus
4. Methane-rich fuel from cow dung | d. yeast

Assertion (A): Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty's work showed how microorganisms could be used to solve environmental problems such as pollution.
Reason (R): His discovery received a patent in 1980.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Snehal wants to find out whether mixing dried leaves into kitchen peels changes how quickly they turn into manure. Plan a fair test with two pits. Give: (a) what she should change between the pits; (b) three things she must keep the same, with a reason linked to how microbes make manure; (c) what she should look for, and when; (d) the result that would show dried leaves speed things up; (e) one way to make her result more trustworthy.
questions.a: (a) Only whether dried leaves are mixed in: pit A peels with dried leaves, pit B the same peels without. (b) Any three: the same amount and kind of peels, the same soil cover, the same moisture, the same place (so the same temperature). Manure forms when fungi and bacteria in the soil break the waste down, and this goes best at an optimal temperature and an appropriate moisture level, so a difference in these could cause the result instead of the leaves. (c) Peels turning into dark-coloured, nutrient-rich manure, checked on the same days in both pits, for example after 2 to 3 weeks. (d) The pit with dried leaves turns into dark manure sooner, or more completely by the same day. (e) Set up two or more pits of each kind (or repeat the test) and compare them on the same days.
s: (a) only the dried leaves differ
(b) three things kept the same, linked to temperature and moisture for microbes
(c) look for dark manure, checked on the same days, about 2 to 3 weeks
(d) the leaf pit forms manure sooner
(e) more than one pit of each kind, or a repeat

questions.q: True or False? 'Growing beans helps only the beans themselves; it leaves no benefit in the soil for the crop that follows.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The root nodules of beans contain Rhizobium bacteria, which trap nitrogen from the air and make it useful for plants. Growing legumes in rotation naturally increases the nitrogen in the soil and keeps it healthy for the next crop, which then needs less chemical fertiliser.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Rhizobium raises soil nitrogen, which benefits the next crop

questions.q: Set curd left on a kitchen counter on a warm May day tastes more sour by evening. Which explanation fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Lactobacillus keeps making lactic acid from milk sugar
o: Lactobacillus keeps making lactic acid from milk sugar
Yeast in the curd goes on making alcohol, which is sour
Warmth dries the curd, so its taste becomes stronger
Lactobacillus dies in the heat, and dead bacteria taste sour

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'Because the bacteria that make the gas live in an oxygen-free environment.' Write a question about turning waste into fuel for which this is the correct answer. Then say what the gas is mainly made of, and give two of its uses.
questions.a: Example question: 'Why must a biogas tank be closed so that air cannot get in?' The gas, biogas, is mainly carbon dioxide with a high proportion of methane. Uses (any two): cooking, heating, generating electricity, running vehicles.
s: A question about why the biogas tank is kept closed or airtight
Biogas is mainly carbon dioxide with a high proportion of methane
Two uses: cooking, heating, electricity or vehicles

questions.q: In 1985 a company wants to sell copies of the oil-eating bacterium that Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty developed in 1971. Going by the chapter's meaning of a patent, what must the company do first?
questions.a: Get Chakrabarty's permission, as his 1980 patent covers it
o: Get Chakrabarty's permission, as his 1980 patent covers it
Nothing, since living things such as bacteria cannot be owned
Nothing, since the bacterium was made before the 1980 patent
Only print Chakrabarty's name on each pack when selling it

questions.q:
(a) In 1971 Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty developed a special bacterium that could break down oil spills. Why does the chapter count this as microbes solving an environmental problem?
(b) The chapter asks what other problems microbes can help solve. Using (a), name one other problem from this chapter that microbes already help with, and say how.
questions.a: (a) An oil spill pollutes the environment; his bacterium broke the oil down and helped clean it, showing that microorganisms can be used against pollution. (b) Any one: waste such as fallen leaves, peels and dung is decomposed by fungi and bacteria into manure; plant and animal waste is turned into biogas, a fuel; Rhizobium in legume nodules traps nitrogen and cuts the need for chemical fertilisers.
s: (a) the bacterium broke down oil pollution and cleaned the environment
(b) another problem microbes help with, and how

questions.q: True or False? 'Only plant waste can be used to make biogas.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Bacteria that live in an oxygen-free environment can decompose plant waste, animal waste (such as dung) and household wastewater, releasing biogas.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: plant waste, animal waste and household wastewater can all give biogas

questions.q:
A farmer near Indore grows the same wheat variety on two equal fields and gets the same yield from both.
Field | Crop grown the season before | Chemical nitrogen fertiliser used for the wheat
1 | wheat | 60 kg
2 | beans | 35 kg
(a) What lives in the swollen parts of bean roots, and what does it do?
(b) Use (a) to explain why Field 2 needed less fertiliser.
(c) Fertiliser costs Rs 30 per kg. How much did the farmer save on Field 2?
(d) For the next two seasons on Field 1, the farmer can grow wheat in both seasons, or beans first and then wheat. He adds no nitrogen fertiliser to beans; wheat after wheat needs 60 kg and wheat after beans needs 35 kg; and a season of beans earns him Rs 4,000 less than a season of wheat. Using the price in (c), does the fertiliser saving from growing beans make up for the lower bean income? Name one benefit that these money figures leave out.
questions.a: (a) Rhizobium bacteria live in the root nodules of legumes such as beans; they trap nitrogen from the air and make it useful for the plants. (b) The beans' Rhizobium increased the nitrogen in the soil naturally, so less had to be added as chemical fertiliser for the next crop. (c) 60 - 35 = 25 kg less; 25 x 30 = Rs 750 saved. (d) Wheat then wheat: 60 + 60 = 120 kg x Rs 30 = Rs 3,600. Beans then wheat: 0 + 35 = 35 kg x Rs 30 = Rs 1,050. Saving = Rs 2,550, which is less than the Rs 4,000 of lost income, so no (short by Rs 1,450). Left out: growing legumes in rotation naturally raises soil nitrogen and keeps the soil healthy for later crops, with less chemical fertiliser.
s: (a) Rhizobium in root nodules traps nitrogen from the air
(b) beans raised soil nitrogen, so less fertiliser was needed
(c) 25 kg x Rs 30 = Rs 750
(d) saving Rs 2,550 is below Rs 4,000; soil health is left out

questions.q:
A dairy co-operative in Anand tests how quickly curd sets. Each bowl gets 500 mL of milk and one spoon of curd and is covered.
Bowl | Where kept | After 4 hours | After 8 hours
P | refrigerator | liquid | liquid, slightly sour
Q | kitchen shelf on a cool winter day | liquid | soft, partly set
R | warm corner near the oven, lukewarm | set | set, more sour
(a) Which bowl matches bowl A of the chapter's activity, and why did it set fastest?
(b) Why has P not set even after 8 hours?
(c) What does bowl Q show that the chapter's two-bowl activity could not show?
(d) Why does the co-operative add a spoon of old curd at all?
(e) It wants curd set within 5 hours every winter morning. Recommend where to keep the bowls, and name one thing it must keep the same in every bowl so that the test is fair.
questions.a: (a) R (lukewarm milk in a warm place). Lactobacillus grows well in warm conditions, so it multiplies fast, feeds on the milk sugar (lactose) and ferments the milk into curd.
