(b) In the cold, the bacteria do not grow well, so too little fermentation takes place for the milk to set (though a little lactic acid can make it slightly sour). (c) Setting depends on how warm it is, not just on warm versus cold: a cool place sets curd slowly and only partly. (d) Curd contains several kinds of bacteria, including Lactobacillus, so the spoon of curd brings the bacteria that ferment the milk. (e) In a warm place such as R's corner, since only R set within 4 to 5 hours; keep the same amount of milk and curd (or the same covering) in every bowl.
s: (a) R: Lactobacillus grows well in warmth and ferments lactose
(b) P: the bacteria grow poorly in the cold
(c) Q shows setting speed depends on how warm it is
(d) the old curd supplies Lactobacillus
(e) a warm place, with the same milk and curd amounts in every bowl

questions.q: When Ravi runs to catch a bus, his nerve cells carry messages while his muscle cells contract and relax. Which idea from the chapter does this best show?
questions.a: Cells of a multicellular body specialise but also cooperate
o: Cells of a multicellular body specialise but also cooperate
Like Amoeba, each of his cells carries out all life functions
His nerve cells and muscle cells share one shape and one job
Every cell in his body can do all of the body's jobs alone

questions.q:
(a) An ostrich egg yolk about 150 mm across and a bacterium about 0.002 mm long are each a single cell. How many times wider is the yolk than the bacterium is long?
(b) Using (a), what does this tell you about using size to decide whether something is a cell?
questions.a: (a) 150 / 0.002 = 75,000 times. (b) Cells differ enormously in size, so size alone cannot tell you whether something is a cell; one cell can be too small to see or as large as an ostrich yolk. What counts is that it is a single unit of life.
s: (b) cells vary hugely in size, so size alone does not decide

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under a powerful microscope, a bacterial cell can be told apart from a yeast cell.
Reason (R): Bacterial cells are not surrounded by a cell membrane.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A self-help group in Kerala sets up a Spirulina tank on Monday 5 January 2026, following the chapter's steps (stir twice a week; harvest after 3 to 6 weeks).
(i) What is the earliest date they can expect to harvest?
(ii) What is the latest date in the harvest window?
(iii) They stir on the set-up day and after that every Monday and Thursday. Counting the set-up day, how many times will the tank have been stirred up to and including the date in (ii)?
questions.a: (i) 3 weeks after 5 January = 26 January 2026. (ii) 6 weeks after 5 January = 16 February 2026. (iii) Six full weeks from Monday 5 January give 6 x 2 = 12 stirrings (Mondays 5 Jan to 9 Feb and Thursdays 8 Jan to 12 Feb); 16 February is also a Monday, so one more: 13 times.
s: (i) 26 January
(ii) 16 February
(iii) 13 stirrings, counting the final Monday

questions.q: Spirulina is rich in protein, more than 60 per cent of its body weight. So a 25 g packet of dried Spirulina contains more than ___ g of protein. (Write the number in digits.)
Give one way in which a fungal cell, such as a mould cell, is like a plant cell, and one way it differs. Then say what the difference means for how the fungus gets food.
questions.a: Alike: both have a cell wall (and a cell membrane). Differ: a fungal cell has no chloroplasts, while green plant cells have chloroplasts. So a fungus cannot make its own food by photosynthesis.
s: Alike: both have a cell wall
Differ: no chloroplasts in fungi, so no photosynthesis

questions.q:
Mohit filled in this table comparing three kinds of cells (yes = present).
Cell | Cell membrane | Cell wall | Well-defined nucleus | Chloroplasts
Plant (leaf) | yes | yes | yes | yes
Animal (cheek) | yes | yes | yes | no
Bacterial | yes | yes | yes | no
His teacher says two entries are wrong, and that the cell wall entries for the plant and bacterial cells are correct.
(a) Find the wrong entry in the animal row and correct it.
(b) Find the wrong entry in the bacterial row, correct it, and say what the bacterial cell has instead.
(c) Which structure in the table is present in all three kinds of cells, and in every microorganism's cell too?
(d) The teacher then shows an unknown cell with a cell membrane, a cell wall and a well-defined nucleus, but no chloroplasts or any other plastids. Decide which group of organisms in the chapter it most likely belongs to, and rule out the plant cell.
questions.a: (a) Cell wall: animal cells such as cheek cells have no cell wall, so it should be 'no'. (b) Well-defined nucleus: bacteria do not have a well-defined nucleus or nuclear membrane, so it should be 'no'; instead they have a nucleoid. (c) The cell membrane: like plant and animal cells, the cells of microorganisms are also surrounded by a cell membrane. (d) A fungus (for example yeast): fungal cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, and unlike bacteria they have a nucleus. It is not a plant cell, because cells in all parts of a plant have plastids, and this cell has none.
s: (a) animal cell wall should be 'no'
(b) bacterial nucleus should be 'no'; they have a nucleoid
(c) the cell membrane
(d) a fungus; not a plant cell, as plant cells always have plastids

questions.q: After the monsoon in Shillong, a tree trunk has a thin green film. Under a microscope it shows tiny green cells. Which conclusion fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Likely microalgae, which live even on trees and use sunlight
o: Likely microalgae, which live even on trees and use sunlight
They must be mould, since mould grows on any damp surface outdoors
They are bacteria, coloured green by the bark they are sitting on
They cannot be living, since microbes live only in water and soil

questions.q: True or False? 'An organism made of just one cell must carry out every function needed for its survival inside that single cell.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Unicellular organisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, carry out all the functions necessary for their survival in a single cell. In multicellular organisms, by contrast, cells carry out specialised functions and cooperate with each other.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a unicellular organism does every survival function in its one cell, unlike specialised body cells

questions.q: Kunal claims: 'Bacteria have no nucleus, so they cannot really be living cells.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Wrong. Bacteria lack a well-defined nucleus and nuclear membrane, but they have a nucleoid instead. They are unicellular organisms: their single cell, surrounded by a cell membrane, carries out all the functions necessary for survival. The chapter says all living beings, including microorganisms, are made up of one or more cells, so a bacterium is a living cell.
s: Verdict: wrong
Bacteria have a nucleoid instead of a well-defined nucleus
Their single cell carries out all life functions, so it is a living cell

questions.q:
Match each fact in Column I with what it leads to in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A microalga's cells contain chlorophyll | a. it can be told apart from yeast, protozoa, algae, plant and animal cells
2. A bacterial cell has a nucleoid instead of a nucleus | b. the organism is multicellular
3. Spirulina is more than 60 per cent protein | c. it makes its own food using sunlight and releases oxygen
4. An organism's cells carry out specialised functions and cooperate | d. it is sold as a health supplement and called a superfood

(a) For a week, a floating plastic sheet blocks the sunlight over one part of a pond. What happens to the oxygen released by the microalgae under the sheet, and why?
(b) Using (a) and the share of Earth's oxygen that microalgae produce, explain why the chapter warns that losing microalgae upsets Earth's oxygen balance.
questions.a: (a) It falls: microalgae release oxygen while making their own food using sunlight, and under the sheet they get no sunlight to do this. (b) Microalgae produce more than half of the Earth's oxygen supply, so if large numbers are lost (to pollution, climate change or habitat destruction) a large share of the oxygen being released is lost too.
s: (a) less oxygen: microalgae release it only while making food with sunlight
(b) they give over half of Earth's oxygen, so losing them upsets the balance

questions.q:
A teacher gives this record of six cells. All six have a cell membrane.
Cell | Cell wall | Well-defined nucleus | Chloroplasts | How it lives
P | yes | yes | yes | part of a green leaf
Q | no | yes | no | part of the inner lining of the cheek
R | yes | no (a nucleoid) | no | a whole organism of one cell
S | no | yes | no | a whole organism of one cell, irregular in shape, moving
T | yes | yes | no | a whole organism of one cell that makes dough rise
U | yes | yes | no | joined with others in branched filaments
Design a key of yes/no questions, using only these features, that ends with each cell on its own. Name each cell where it lands, and finish by explaining how the record supports the statement 'the cell is the basic unit of life'.
questions.a: One sound key: (1) 'Does it have a well-defined nucleus?' No: R, a bacterium. (2) Yes: 'Does it have a cell wall?' No: Q and S. (3) For Q and S: 'Is it a whole organism by itself?' Yes: S, Amoeba (unicellular); no: Q, a cheek cell, one specialised cell of a multicellular body. (4) Cell wall yes: 'Does it have chloroplasts?' Yes: P, a leaf cell; no: T and U, fungi. 'Does it live as a single cell?' Yes: T, yeast; no: U, mould. (5) Every cell has a cell membrane and its own working parts; in R, S and T one cell is the whole organism doing every job, while P, Q and U are units of many-celled bodies, so all life, from bacteria to plants and humans, is built from cells.
s: A first question that separates the bacterium by its nucleoid
A cell-wall question that separates Q and S from P, T and U
Q and S told apart, named cheek cell and Amoeba
P, T and U told apart, named leaf cell, yeast and mould
Shared membrane and one-cell versus many-cell organisms used to support the statement

questions.q: Under a high-powered microscope, a cell shows a cell membrane and a cell wall, but no well-defined nucleus; instead there is a nucleoid region. What is it most likely to be?
questions.a: A bacterium
o: A bacterium
A yeast cell
An Amoeba
A cell of an alga

questions.q:
A school microscope magnifies at most 400 times; an electron microscope magnifies a cell about 10,00,000 times. A detail can be made out only if it looks at least 1 mm across.
(i) How many times greater is the electron microscope's magnification?
(ii) How large would a structure 0.0001 mm across look under each?
(iii) Use (ii) and the 1 mm rule to explain why the chapter says we need microscopes with high magnification to see the parts inside a cell.
questions.a: (i) 10,00,000 / 400 = 2500 times greater. (ii) School microscope: 0.0001 x 400 = 0.04 mm; electron microscope: 0.0001 x 10,00,000 = 100 mm. (iii) 0.04 mm is far below 1 mm, so the structure cannot be made out with the school microscope; 100 mm is well above 1 mm, so the electron microscope shows it. Structures inside a cell need such very high magnification.
s: (i) 2500 times
(ii) 0.04 mm and 100 mm
(iii) 0.04 mm is below 1 mm but 100 mm is above it, so high magnification is needed

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: Yeast is a unicellular fungus, while mould is a multicellular fungus.
Statement 2: Bacteria have a well-defined nucleus surrounded by a nuclear membrane.
Statement 3: Microalgae produce less than a quarter of the Earth's oxygen supply.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
(a) Microalgae are described as plant-like. Give two ways in which they are like plants, using the chapter.
(b) Using (a), explain why they are still counted among the microorganisms rather than with plants such as trees.
questions.a: (a) They make their own food using sunlight, and while doing so they release oxygen (they also have chlorophyll, as the algae in the soil record do). (b) Being plant-like is about how they get food; a microorganism is a living being too small to be seen with the naked eye, and microalgae are microscopic, made of one or a few cells.
s: (a) they make food using sunlight and release oxygen
(b) they are microscopic, which is what makes them microorganisms

questions.q:
A science museum in Delhi is making a wall of five cards about how many cells living things have: yeast, mould, a bacterium, Amoeba and a human. Each card must say whether the organism is unicellular or multicellular. The designer also wants to add the heading 'Cells that specialise and cooperate', backed by examples that a visitor can check in this chapter.
(a) Which of the five organisms are unicellular?
(b) Which two belong to the same group of microorganisms but differ in the number of cells?
(c) The heading fits only one card. Should it go on the human card or the mould card? Decide, and say whether the other multicellular card could honestly carry it too.
questions.a: (a) Yeast, the bacterium and Amoeba. (b) Yeast and mould: both are fungi, but yeast is unicellular and mould is multicellular. (c) The human card: the chapter names specialised human cells a visitor can check, such as spindle-shaped muscle cells, long branched nerve cells and thin flat cheek cells, and says the cells of multicellular organisms specialise and cooperate. The mould card is covered by that general statement, since mould is multicellular, so the heading would not be false there; but the chapter describes no specialised mould cells, so it could not be backed with examples.
s: (a) yeast, bacterium, Amoeba
(b) yeast and mould, both fungi
(c) the human card, with checkable examples; mould fits the general rule but has no examples

A women's self-help group near Mysuru writes this draft plan for Spirulina farming, starting on 10 August:
Step 1: Place the clear glass tank on the open roof in full afternoon sun.
Step 2: Fill the tank with tap water.
Step 3: Add living Spirulina collected from a pond.
Step 4: Stir the tank once a month.
Step 5: Harvest on 20 August by filtering through a fine cloth.
Step 6: Sell it with the label 'More than 80 per cent protein'.
Five of the six steps disagree with the chapter. For each of the five, say what is wrong and write the corrected step; for the harvest step, give the correct harvest window as dates.
questions.a: Step 1: wrong; set the tank in a bright place away from direct sunlight, covered with a shade net or kept at a moderate temperature. Step 2: wrong; fill the tank with pond water. Step 4: wrong; stir twice a week. Step 5: wrong; harvest after 3 to 6 weeks, that is between 31 August and 21 September, by filtering through a fine cloth. Step 6: wrong; Spirulina is rich in protein, more than 60 per cent of its body weight, so the label should say 'more than 60 per cent protein'. Step 3 is correct.
s: Step 1 corrected: bright place, away from direct sun, shade net or moderate temperature
Step 2 corrected: pond water
Step 4 corrected: stir twice a week
Step 5 corrected: harvest window 31 August to 21 September
Step 6 corrected: more than 60 per cent protein

questions.q:
A lake near Bengaluru supports many fish. A college survey counts the microalgae in one drop of lake water each year.
Year | Microalgae counted per drop
2022 | 8000
2024 | 5000
2026 | 2000
Waste water from a nearby factory has been flowing into the lake since 2021.
(a) By what percentage did the count fall from 2022 to 2026?
(b) Give two jobs microalgae do that matter for the fish in the lake.
(c) Which threat to microalgae named in the chapter does the factory waste water represent?
(d) The village council can fund only one plan this year. Plan 1: a unit that cleans the factory waste water before it reaches the lake (Rs 8 lakh; the lake is expected to recover slowly over a few years). Plan 2: release 5,000 young fish now (Rs 1 lakh) to raise next year's catch; young fish in this lake feed on microalgae and on the tiny animals that eat microalgae. Decide, using (a) and (b), and say what the council gives up with its choice.
questions.a: (a) Fall = 8000 - 2000 = 6000; 6000 / 8000 x 100 = 75 per cent. (b) Microalgae are a food source for many aquatic animals, and they release oxygen while making their food. (c) Pollution. (d) Plan 1 is the better choice: the microalgae that feed the lake's animals and release oxygen have already fallen by 75 per cent, and the young fish in Plan 2 would depend on that same shrinking food supply, so many might not survive while the pollution continues. Plan 1 removes the cause. What is given up: Plan 2 is far cheaper (Rs 1 lakh against Rs 8 lakh) and would raise the catch at once, while Plan 1 brings recovery only slowly.
s: (a) 75 per cent
(b) food for aquatic animals and oxygen release
(c) pollution
(d) a plan chosen using the 75 per cent fall and food supply, naming what is given up
